texts.full_text: == A diverse collection of mitochondrial diseases have been linked to mutations that affect either mitochondrial or nuclear genomes, and alter respiratory chain function, mitochondrial fission/fusion cycles, or mitochondrial quality control ([@bib40]). A central feature of mitochondrial disease is the pleotropic nature of phenotypes, with some diseases eliciting highly tissue-specific effects and others affecting multiple organ systems. The basis of this pleiotropy is poorly understood, but could reflect differences in mitochondrial structure and concomitant links with respiratory chain activity within individual tissues ([@bib40]). Proper organization of the respiratory chain and other mitochondrial protein complexes within the mitochondrial inner membrane (MIM) relies on the formaton and function of the mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system (MICOS). The MICOS complex is an integral component of the MIM architecture that facilitates formation of contact sites between the inner and outer membranes, thereby promoting close apposition with respiratory chain protein complexes ([@bib41]). Mutations in several genes encoding subunits of this multi-subunit structure have been linked to mitochondrial disease ([@bib42]), highlighting its importance for proper assembly of the respiratory chain. For example, a recent study reported that mutations in MIC60 (encoded by ) disrupt normal cristae architecture and lead to severe mtDNA depletion syndrome with liver failure as an early manifestation ([@bib13]). In addition, recessive loss-of-function mutations affecting have been associated with severe mitochondrial myopathy characterized by impaired oxidative phosphorylation capacity in skeletal muscle fibers along with elevated lactate levels ([@bib43]). These signals trigger the fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane, a process known as exocytosis, which releases the digestive enzymes and other proteins into the pancreatic duct and subsequently into the duodenum. Later, in Ellsworth, Maine, she started a millinery business and became actively involved in religious life, joining the local Unitarian church. In 1880, she married another member of her church, Millard Fillmore Avery, and shortly later moved to Boston, Massachusetts. Boston and socialism Boston exposed her to a much wider range of religious and social thought. There she studied metaphysics with Charles D. Sherman, an astrologer and student of Eastern thought. She also joined the Nationalist Club, a local society created to promote the ideas of socialist utopian author Edward Bellamy. Her involvements in this club included working on a plan for a "Woman's Commonwealth" that would serve as a socialist model community. In 1890, Avery and her husband joined the newly formed Society of Christian Socialists, where she began to advocate for socialism within Christianity. However, her faith was shaken after reading Edward Bellamy's "Looking Backward," which presented a vision of a socialist utopia without God. This led her to explore other religions, including Buddhism and Theosophy, but she eventually found herself drawn back to Christianity through the works of Charles Kingsley and Frederic Denison Maurice. Conversion and Anti-Socialism Activism: In 1894, Avery converted to Catholicism under the influence of Monsignor Thomas J. Shahan at the Catholic University of America. This conversion marked a significant shift in her ideological stance as she now actively opposed socialism. She believed that socialist teachings were incompatible with Christian morality due to their materialist and atheist tendencies. Avery founded the Common Cause Society, which aimed to promote social justice from a Catholic perspective and counter socialist influence among workers. texts.full_text: The Guardian's film critic, Peter Bradshaw, calls him "flawed, vulnerable, human, committed to his craft," while just about every other blogger says things like the story is a "savage parody of self-important film bloggers," or the character is "self-absorbed," or he's "driven by a combination of loneliness and narcissism," or the strip is look at internet geeks who think that anyone cares what they post on their review blogs." Ouch.If anyone cares what I post on my blog, I also think "Justin M. Damiano" goes deeper than the non-film-critic critics would have you believe. Critics rest so uneasily on the periphery of art that making them its subject usually results in some kind of long-suppressed catharsis (click the link to Bradshaw's blog entry for proof). However, Clowes is a master of the peripheral, and that's why I can't believe Damiano is just another dart aimed to deflate critical puffery.But then, as a theater critic/blogger, maybe, like Bradshaw, I've got too much in common with Damiano himself to clearly read Clowes' intentions. Or maybe I got that window all fogged up again. Either way, and for whatever it reveals about the critical temperament, I'll say this much: once again, Dan Clowes has proven himself a portraitist.
